name: Honey and beetroot lip remedies

card.summary: Folk remedies using honey or beetroot juice for lip color and softness; beetroot stains temporarily, and no lip studies exist.
card.note: Honey and beet products can cause allergic reactions in some people.

quick.overview:
Honey and beetroot are used in home lip remedies. Honey is applied for moisture, beetroot juice as a natural pink-red tint.

No studies of either for changing lip color were found.
quick.mechanism: Beetroot's red pigment is betanin, a betalain used industrially as a red food colorant.[2] Honey has been studied as a wound dressing.[1]
quick.risks: Honey can interact with existing allergies according to Wikipedia, and honey is not recommended for infants under one year when eaten.[1]

lead: Honey and beetroot lip remedies are home practices for softer, rosier-looking lips: honey is applied for moisture and smoothness, and beetroot juice is dabbed on as a temporary pink-to-red tint. Home-beauty guides commonly combine them, mixing beet juice with honey and a fat such as coconut oil into a homemade tinted balm.

Beetroot owes its red colour to betanin, a betalain pigment extracted from beet juice and used commercially as a red food colourant, listed as E162. [2][4] Honey is a long-standing folk treatment for burns and skin injuries; it has antibacterial activity in laboratory settings and preliminary evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns, though these findings concern wound care and not lip colour. [1]

For looks, the payoff is plain: lips that look smoother and carry a natural-looking tint without lipstick. The colour is temporary, as betanin stains skin and washes off, and no published study of either substance for lip appearance was identified.

chain: Honey coats the lips and holds moisture
Beetroot's betanin pigment stains the surface of the lips pink to red
Smoother-looking lips with a temporary natural tint
angle.text: People dab beet juice on the lips for a rosy stain and use honey as a moisturising layer, producing a softer look and a tint that lasts until it wears off.

paras: Honey is a long-standing folk treatment for burns and skin injuries. Evidence for most wound uses is low quality, and the FDA has approved several medical-grade honey products for minor wounds and burns. [1] Honey is used on lips as a natural humectant in home recipes, in the same role that occlusive waxes and petrolatum play in commercial lip balms, which seal in moisture and protect thin lip skin from dry air and wind. [3]

Betanin is the red pigment in beetroot and is used in foods such as sauces, desserts and candy. [2] Its colour depends on pH, appearing bluish-red around pH 4 to 5 and shifting toward blue-violet as pH rises, and it degrades with light, heat and oxygen. [4] Wikipedia reports no safety concerns for betanin as a food additive and no link to clinical food allergy when used as a colourant, while a European Food Safety Authority panel found toxicity data too limited for conclusive evaluation. [4] The betanin article does not mention cosmetic uses. Eating beetroot can turn urine or stool reddish, which is harmless. [2]

Lips have thin tissue and no sweat glands, so they dry and chap easily. [5] Natural lip colour depends on blood visible through thin tissue and on melanin content. [5] Commercial lip balms combine waxes such as beeswax with ingredients such as petrolatum and may include colourants or sunscreen; some experts say fragrance in flavoured balms can irritate lip skin. [3]
